title: Data Warehouse
seoTitle: Design a Data Warehouse for Business Intelligence
description: Design a data warehouse for business intelligence — ingesting from operational databases and events, ELT into layered models, columnar storage and partitioning, a semantic layer for consistent metrics, and fast BI dashboards.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Data Warehouse?
blocks.text: A data warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, or one built on a lakehouse) is where a company brings together data from all its systems — orders, payments, marketing, product events — to answer business questions: "revenue by region last quarter", "conversion by acquisition channel". BI tools like Looker or Tableau query it for dashboards. It's built for scanning and aggregating billions of rows, not for serving individual app requests.

items: Ingest data from operational databases, SaaS tools and event streams.
Transform raw data into clean, modelled tables (facts and dimensions) on a schedule.
Analysts and BI dashboards should run SQL queries over years of history.
Business metrics ("active customer", "net revenue") should have one consistent definition everywhere.
Access should be controlled down to tables, columns and rows.
Real-time operational analytics (seconds-fresh; see Ad Click Aggregator).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Freshness: most data within an hour; daily for some sources.
Dashboards load in a few seconds; ad-hoc queries over billions of rows in tens of seconds.
Correct and trustworthy: data quality checks catch broken pipelines before dashboards show wrong numbers.
Scale to petabytes and hundreds of concurrent users without one heavy query slowing everyone.
Cost-aware: storage is cheap, compute is not.
Transactional consistency with source systems at every instant.
**Source**: an operational system or stream feeding the warehouse.
**Raw table**: data as ingested, append-only, partitioned by load time.
**Model**: a transformation (SQL) producing a cleaned table, with dependencies on other tables.
**Fact table**: events or transactions (orders, payments) with keys and measures.
**Dimension table**: descriptive attributes (customer, product, date), possibly versioned over time.
**Metric**: a named, governed definition (e.g. `net_revenue = sum(amount) - refunds`).

blocks.code:
(ingestion) CDC from databases; connectors for SaaS APIs; Kafka -> object storage
(transform) models as SQL in version control, run by a scheduler/DAG
(query)     SQL endpoint (JDBC/ODBC) for BI tools and analysts
(semantic)  GET /metrics/net_revenue?by=region&from=&to=

blocks.text: Operational databases are replicated with **change data capture** (reading the database log) rather than nightly full dumps, so ingestion is incremental and doesn't load the source. SaaS sources are pulled by connectors; product events stream through Kafka. Everything lands in a **raw layer** in columnar files on object storage, unchanged.

Transformations run **inside the warehouse** (ELT) as SQL models in version control: **staging** (clean types, rename, dedupe), **core** (facts and dimensions in a star schema), and **marts** (aggregates for specific teams). A DAG scheduler (Airflow, dbt) runs models in dependency order, incrementally where possible.

Tables are stored in a **columnar** format (Parquet or the warehouse's native format) compressed per column, and **partitioned** (by date) and **clustered** (by common filter columns) so queries read only the needed columns and partitions. A **massively parallel** query engine splits each query across many workers.
A **semantic layer** defines metrics and dimensions once ("net revenue", "region"), and BI tools query through it, so every dashboard computes revenue the same way.
1) How do we make BI queries fast?

approach.text: Run analytics directly on the production Postgres replica.

challenges.text: Row-oriented storage scans whole rows; big queries take minutes and compete with the app.

approach.text: Store data in columnar, compressed tables partitioned by date and processed by an MPP engine.

challenges.text: Popular dashboards still re-scan large fact tables on every load.

approach.text: Add **pre-aggregated** tables or materialised views for common dashboard queries (daily revenue by region), refreshed incrementally; enable **result caching** for repeated queries; and separate **compute clusters** per workload (BI dashboards, ad-hoc analysts, heavy transformations) over the same shared storage, so a giant analyst query can't slow down executive dashboards. Compute scales up and down with demand to control cost.

challenges.text: Pre-aggregates must be kept consistent with the underlying facts — derive them in the same DAG.

blocks.text: 2) How do we keep data trustworthy?

Every model has **tests**: uniqueness of keys, non-null columns, referential integrity, and row-count and freshness checks against expectations. Failing tests stop downstream models and alert owners, so dashboards show "data delayed" rather than wrong numbers. **Lineage** (which tables feed which dashboards) lets teams see the impact of a broken source, and **data contracts** with source teams catch breaking schema changes before they ship.
Mention slowly changing dimensions: when a customer moves region, decide whether past orders report under the old or new region — keep history with versioned dimension rows (SCD type 2).

Sensitive columns (emails, payment details) are **masked** or tokenised for most roles; **row-level security** restricts, for example, regional managers to their region. Access is granted to roles, not individuals, and every query is logged for audits. Personal data deletion requests (GDPR) propagate through raw and modelled layers by key.

quiz.question: Why use columnar storage for analytics?
options: Queries read only the columns they need, and columns compress well
quiz.explanation: Analytical queries scan few columns across many rows.

quiz.question: What does CDC provide for ingestion?
options: Incremental changes from the database log without heavy full dumps
quiz.explanation: Reading the log captures every change with low source impact.

quiz.question: What is the semantic layer for?
options: Defining metrics once so every dashboard calculates them the same way
quiz.explanation: Consistent definitions build trust in numbers.

quiz.question: Why separate compute clusters per workload?
options: So heavy ad-hoc queries don't slow dashboards or transformations
quiz.explanation: Shared storage with isolated compute avoids noisy neighbours.
